title: Lysistrata
creator: Aristophanes
description: Aristophanes' anti-war sex-strike comedy was treated as obscene for two millennia: expurgated from school texts, seized by US Customs and barred from the mails under the Comstock regime; this is the unexpurgated Athenian Society translation.

title: Letters on the English
creator: Voltaire
description: Voltaire's Letters on the English (Lettres philosophiques, 1733/34) praised English liberty against French absolutism; the Parlement of Paris ordered the book seized and burned by the public hangman and a warrant issued for the author.

title: Caleb Williams
creator: William Godwin
description: Godwin's Caleb Williams (1794), a novel of persecution by aristocratic power written to embody Political Justice, appeared in the year of the Treason Trials; its preface was suppressed in the first edition as too dangerous to print.

title: Fruits of Philosophy
creator: Charles Knowlton
description: Knowlton's Fruits of Philosophy (1832), the first American birth-control manual, brought its author a prison sentence in Massachusetts; its 1877 London republication caused the famous Bradlaugh-Besant obscenity trial.

title: The Law of Population
creator: Annie Besant
description: Annie Besant's Law of Population (1877), written after the Knowlton trial, argued contraception was a moral duty; the pamphlet was seized and its sellers prosecuted in the obscenity regime of the era.

title: Woman and the New Race
creator: Margaret Sanger
description: Sanger's Woman and the New Race (1920) argued contraception was the key to women's emancipation; Sanger had fled a Comstock indictment for The Woman Rebel and her books and clinics were raided through the 1920s.

title: The Pivot of Civilization
creator: Margaret Sanger
description: Sanger's Pivot of Civilization (1922) pressed the case for birth control against church and state opposition; her lectures were repeatedly banned by police and her 1921 Town Hall meeting was raided on a bishop's complaint.

title: Wise Parenthood
creator: Marie Carmichael Stopes
description: Stopes's Wise Parenthood (1918), the practical sequel to Married Love, gave explicit contraceptive instruction; it was banned in the United States and seized as obscene under the Comstock regime.

title: Married Love
creator: Marie Carmichael Stopes
description: Stopes's Married Love (1918), a frank guide to sexual fulfilment in marriage, was banned in the United States until a 1931 court ruling and treated as contraband under the Comstock laws.

title: Index Librorum Prohibitorum (1917 edition)
creator: Catholic Church. Congregation of the Index
description: The Vatican's Index of Prohibited Books in its 1917 codified edition - the official catalogue of banned literature, listing by name the works Catholics were forbidden to read, from Erasmus and Galileo to Gibbon and Renan.

title: Underground Russia
creator: Stepniak (Sergey Kravchinsky)
description: Stepniak's Underground Russia (1883), profiles of Nihilist revolutionaries by a participant who had assassinated the Tsar's police chief, was banned in Russia and became the West's window on the revolutionary underground.

title: Queen Mab: A Philosophical Poem
creator: Percy Bysshe Shelley
description: Shelley's Queen Mab (1813), his atheist-materialist epic attacking kings, priests and commerce, was printed privately after booksellers refused it; pirated editions brought blasphemy prosecutions on its publishers for twenty years.

title: The Ruins: Or, Meditation on the Revolutions of Empires
creator: Constantin Volney
description: Volney's Ruins (1791), a visionary survey of fallen empires and the common origin of religions, became the deist handbook of the revolutionary era; its translators and publishers faced blasphemy-era suppression and clerical boycotts.

title: An History of the Corruptions of Christianity
creator: Joseph Priestley
description: Priestley's History of the Corruptions of Christianity (1782) argued the early church had been corrupted into Trinitarian orthodoxy; in 1791 a Church-and-King mob burned Priestley's house and laboratory in Birmingham.

title: The System of Nature
creator: Baron d'Holbach (as 'Mirabaud')
description: The System of Nature (1770), the 'bible of atheism', was published under a dead man's name with a false imprint; condemned by the Parlement of Paris to be burned and smuggled across Europe at mortal risk to its sellers.

title: A Confession and What I Believe
creator: Leo Tolstoy
description: Tolstoy's A Confession (written 1879-80) and What I Believe, in Aylmer Maude's translation (World's Classics). Both were banned in Russia: the Confession was confiscated before publication and What I Believe was prohibited, the two texts circulating in secret copies for years.

title: Napoleon the Little
creator: Victor Hugo
description: Hugo's Napoleon the Little (1852), his savage indictment of Louis-Napoleon's coup d'etat, was banned in France and smuggled across the Channel in false bindings by the exiled author's network.

title: History of the Commune of 1871
creator: Prosper-Olivier Lissagaray
description: Lissagaray's History of the Commune (1876), written by a Communard exile from participants' testimony, was banned in France until the amnesty; the English translation by Eleanor Marx (1886) carried the suppressed account abroad.

title: The Saint
creator: Antonio Fogazzaro
description: Fogazzaro's novel The Saint (Il Santo, 1905), about a lay reformer of the Church, was placed on the Index Librorum Prohibitorum in 1906 at the height of the anti-Modernist campaign.

title: Native Life in South Africa
creator: Solomon T. Plaatje
description: Plaatje's Native Life in South Africa (1916), the first book by a black South African in English, protested the 1913 Natives Land Act; the South African authorities suppressed its circulation at home.

title: Southern Horrors: Lynch Law in All Its Phases
creator: Ida B. Wells-Barnett
description: Wells's Southern Horrors (1892) exposed lynching as economic terror; months before, a Memphis mob had destroyed her newspaper office and she wrote the pamphlet in exile, unable to return South on pain of death.

title: The Canton Speech
creator: Eugene V. Debs
description: Debs's Canton Speech of 16 June 1918, opposing conscription and the war, was the evidence that sent him to federal prison for ten years under the Espionage Act; the speech itself was suppressed from the mails as seditious literature.

title: The Life of Lazarillo de Tormes
creator: Anonymous
description: Lazarillo de Tormes (1554), the first picaresque novel, was placed on the Spanish Index in 1559 for its anti-clerical satire and could be printed in Spain only in an expurgated edition for two centuries.

title: A Civic Biology
creator: George William Hunter
description: Hunter's A Civic Biology (1914) was the textbook at the center of the 1925 Scopes trial: Tennessee's Butler Act banned teaching evolution from it, and anti-evolution statutes drove it and its successors from Southern classrooms.

title: Siberia and the Exile System, Volume 1
creator: George Kennan
description: Kennan's Siberia and the Exile System (1891), the Century magazine expose of Tsarist penal exile, was banned in Russia; Kennan himself was expelled from the empire in 1901 for his reporting. Volume 1.

title: Siberia and the Exile System, Volume 2
creator: George Kennan
description: Volume 2 of Kennan's banned-in-Russia expose of the Tsarist exile system (1891), documenting the Kara penal colony and the political prisoners whose testimony the regime suppressed.

title: Ann Veronica
creator: H. G. Wells
description: Wells's novel of a young woman who defies her father, studies biology and demands the vote was denounced from pulpits, removed by lending libraries and effectively banned as immoral on its 1909 publication.

title: Fewer and better babies : birth control, or, The limitations of offspring by prevenception
creator: Robinson, William J. (William Josephus), 1867-1936
description: Birth-control literature of the Comstock era: 'Fewer and better babies : birth control, or, The limitations of offspring by prevenception' (1926) by Robinson, William J. (William Josephus), 1867-1936 circulated while contraceptive information was criminalised as obscenity in the United States and prosecuted in Britain; such works were seized from the mails and their publishers jailed.

creator: Gerrard, Thomas John, 1871-1916
description: Thomas Gerrard's The Church and Eugenics (1917) set out the Catholic case against the birth-control and eugenics movements - a document of the clerical opposition under which contraceptive literature was prosecuted as obscenity.

title: Abstract
creator: A single action-conditioned latent predictive architecture can in principle be trained on the structured state of a driving scene, a robot workspace, or a financial order book. The ingredients for doing so within any one of these domains already exist and are individually validated: masked-latent prediction [1, 2], action-conditioned latent world models [3, 8, 9], discrete action tokenization [4, 5, 6], and joint-embedding prediction on voxelized state [14, 15, 17]. What is not established, and what TERRA addresses, is the transfer question: when does a representation or predictor learned in one structured-state domain carry over to a structurally analogous but otherwise unrelated domain, and by how much. We give this question a formal treatment. We model each domain as a controlled Markov process on a graded latent grid, factor any instantiation into thin domain adapters and a shared domain-invariant core, and identify a cross-domain correspondence with an approximate Markov decision process homomorphism [21, 23, 24] whose quality is measured by a lax bisimulation discrepancy [24, 27] and, at the level of whole domains lacking a shared coordinate system, by a Gromov-Wasserstein distance between their action-conditioned transition operators [29]. Under a Lipschitz predictor we derive a predictive transfer bound that separates source-model error from structural mismatch, grows geometrically in the prediction horizon, and is certified from below by the Gromov-Wasserstein distance; we then connect latent error to decision regret through the Lipschitz value property of bisimulation metrics [21, 22, 25]. The resulting Structured-State Transfer Hypothesis is stated as a falsifiable claim with a preregistered experimental program, centered on a transfer test from driving scenes to order books, including the conditions under which the claim is refuted. We present no empirical results: this is a research proposal whose contribution is to convert a widely repeated intuition into testable theory.
